title: Classification & Biodiversity
description: How scientists group and name organisms — the five kingdoms, vertebrates vs invertebrates, classification keys, binomial naming, and why biodiversity matters.

notes.heading: Why Do We Classify Organisms?
notes.body: Classification (taxonomy) is the science of grouping organisms based on shared characteristics. There are an estimated 8.7 million species on Earth — only about 1.2 million have been formally described. Without a classification system, studying biodiversity would be chaotic. Classification helps scientists: identify unknown organisms, understand evolutionary relationships, predict characteristics of newly discovered species based on their group, and communicate unambiguously across languages. The modern classification system was developed by Carl Linnaeus in the 18th century. He introduced the binomial naming system (each species has a two-part Latin name, e.g., Homo sapiens) and grouped organisms into a hierarchy: Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species. A useful mnemonic: 'King Philip Came Over For Good Soup.' The more classification levels two organisms share, the more closely related they are evolutionarily.

illustration.alt: A pyramid showing the classification hierarchy from kingdom to species with the mnemonic King Philip Came Over For Good Soup.
illustration.caption: The hierarchy runs from broadest (kingdom) to most specific (species); more shared levels mean closer evolutionary relationships.

notes.heading: The Five Kingdoms
notes.body: All living organisms are classified into five kingdoms based on cell type, number of cells, and mode of nutrition: (1) Animals (Animalia) — multicellular, eukaryotic, no cell walls, heterotrophic (eat other organisms), most can move. Examples: mammals, birds, fish, insects, worms. (2) Plants (Plantae) — multicellular, eukaryotic, have cellulose cell walls, autotrophic (photosynthesise using chloroplasts), cannot move. Examples: mosses, ferns, conifers, flowering plants. (3) Fungi — most are multicellular (except yeast), eukaryotic, have chitin cell walls, heterotrophic (saprophytic — feed by digesting dead matter externally then absorbing nutrients). Examples: mushrooms, moulds, yeast. (4) Protists (Protoctista) — mostly unicellular, eukaryotic, diverse nutrition (some photosynthesise like algae, some consume like amoeba). Examples: amoeba, euglena, paramecium, algae. (5) Bacteria (Monera/Prokaryota) — unicellular, prokaryotic (no membrane-bound nucleus), have a cell wall (not cellulose), diverse nutrition. Examples: E. coli, Salmonella, Lactobacillus. Viruses are NOT included in any kingdom — they are not considered alive because they cannot reproduce independently, have no cellular structure, and show no life processes outside a host cell.

illustration.alt: Diagram showing the five kingdoms of life with key features for animals, plants, fungi, protists, and bacteria.
illustration.caption: Organisms are grouped into five kingdoms based on cell type, number of cells, and how they obtain nutrition.

notes.heading: Vertebrates: The Five Classes
notes.body: Vertebrates are animals with a backbone (vertebral column). They belong to the phylum Chordata and are divided into five classes: (1) Fish — aquatic, have gills for gas exchange, most have scales, fins for movement, lay eggs in water, ectothermic (cold-blooded — body temperature varies with environment). Examples: salmon, shark, clownfish. (2) Amphibians — begin life in water (larvae have gills), undergo metamorphosis to become air-breathing adults with lungs and moist skin. Lay eggs in water with no hard shell. Ectothermic. Examples: frog, toad, salamander. (3) Reptiles — have dry, scaly skin to reduce water loss. Lay eggs with leathery shells on land; some give birth to live young. Breathe with lungs throughout life. Ectothermic. Examples: snake, lizard, turtle, crocodile. (4) Birds — have feathers, a beak (no teeth), and forelimbs modified as wings. Lay hard-shelled eggs. Endothermic (warm-blooded — maintain constant body temperature). Examples: eagle, penguin, sparrow. (5) Mammals — have hair or fur, produce milk from mammary glands to feed young, give birth to live young (most — exceptions: platypus and echidna lay eggs). Have different types of teeth (incisors, canines, molars). Endothermic. Examples: human, whale, bat, kangaroo.

illustration.alt: Diagram showing the five vertebrate classes with key features: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals.
illustration.caption: All vertebrates share a backbone; the classes are distinguished by skin covering, egg type, and temperature regulation.

notes.heading: Invertebrates: Major Groups
notes.body: Invertebrates are animals without a backbone — they make up over 95% of all animal species. Major groups: (1) Arthropods — the largest animal phylum. Jointed legs, segmented body, hard exoskeleton (chitin). Divided into: Insects (3 body sections — head/thorax/abdomen, 6 legs, often have wings, e.g., ant, butterfly, beetle); Arachnids (2 body sections, 8 legs, e.g., spider, scorpion, tick); Crustaceans (mostly aquatic, 5+ pairs of legs, 2 pairs of antennae, e.g., crab, lobster, woodlouse); Myriapods (many body segments, many legs, e.g., centipede, millipede). (2) Molluscs — soft body, often protected by a hard shell. Examples: snail (gastropods), clam/oyster (bivalves — two-part hinged shell), octopus/squid (cephalopods — intelligent, no external shell). (3) Annelids — segmented worms with ring-like body segments. Examples: earthworm, leech. (4) Cnidarians — have stinging cells (nematocysts) to capture prey. Radial symmetry. Examples: jellyfish, sea anemone, coral. (5) Echinoderms — spiny skin, radial symmetry (typically 5-part), tube feet for movement. Examples: starfish, sea urchin, sea cucumber.

illustration.alt: Diagram showing major invertebrate groups including arthropods, molluscs, annelids, cnidarians, and echinoderms.
illustration.caption: Invertebrates lack a backbone and include over 95% of animal species, with arthropods being the largest phylum.

notes.heading: Using Classification Keys (Dichotomous Keys)
notes.body: A dichotomous key is a tool used to identify unknown organisms. It consists of a series of paired statements (dichotomous = 'divided into two parts'). Each step presents two contrasting choices (e.g., 'Does the organism have wings?' → Yes/No). By following the choices that match the specimen, you narrow down until you reach its identity. Constructing a key: (1) Start with the most general, easily observable feature. (2) Each pair of statements must be mutually exclusive — the organism must clearly fit one option, not both. (3) Avoid vague terms like 'big' or 'small' — use measurable, objective criteria. (4) Each branch should eventually lead to a single identification. Example: 1a. Has feathers → go to 2; 1b. No feathers → go to 3; 2a. Can fly → House Sparrow; 2b. Cannot fly → Penguin. Branching keys (tree diagrams) show the same information visually. Keys work best when you have a limited set of known possibilities and clear, observable characteristics.

illustration.alt: A branching dichotomous key example that identifies an organism as a sparrow, penguin, or bat based on observable traits.
illustration.caption: Each step gives two contrasting choices; following the matching branch narrows down the organism's identity.

notes.heading: Binomial Naming System
notes.body: The binomial naming system, created by Carl Linnaeus, gives every species a unique two-part scientific name in Latin (or Latinised form). Format: Genus name (capitalised) + species name (lowercase), both italicised when typed or underlined when handwritten. Example: Homo sapiens (human), Panthera leo (lion), Canis lupus (grey wolf). The genus name is shared by closely related species. For instance, Panthera leo (lion) and Panthera tigris (tiger) are in the same genus but different species. This system solves the problem of common names: a 'robin' in the UK is Erithacus rubecula; a 'robin' in North America is Turdus migratorius — they are completely different birds. Scientific names are universal — a biologist in any country, speaking any language, can identify the exact species. The name often describes the organism (e.g., Erythroxylum coca — 'red wood coca', referring to its reddish wood) or honours a person or location.

illustration.alt: Diagram explaining the two-part binomial naming format with examples such as Homo sapiens and Panthera leo.
illustration.caption: Scientific names are universal: the capitalised genus groups closely related species, while the lowercase species name is unique.

notes.heading: Biodiversity and Its Importance
notes.body: Biodiversity (biological diversity) encompasses three levels: (1) Species diversity — the variety of different species in an area. Tropical rainforests and coral reefs have the highest species diversity. (2) Genetic diversity — the variation in genes within a species. High genetic diversity helps populations survive diseases and environmental changes. (3) Ecosystem diversity — the variety of habitats, communities, and ecological processes. Why biodiversity matters: Ecosystem services — pollination (bees, butterflies pollinate ~75% of crop species), water purification (wetlands filter pollutants), soil formation, climate regulation (forests absorb CO₂), pest control (predators regulate prey populations). Resources — food (wild crop relatives provide genetic material for improving agricultural varieties), medicines (~40% of pharmaceuticals derive from natural compounds, e.g., aspirin from willow bark, taxol from yew trees). Ethical/cultural — many people believe species have intrinsic value and a right to exist. Economic — ecotourism, fisheries, timber. Threats to biodiversity: habitat loss (deforestation, urbanisation), climate change, pollution, overexploitation, invasive species. The current extinction rate is estimated to be 100-1,000 times higher than the natural background rate — many scientists refer to this as the sixth mass extinction.

illustration.alt: Diagram showing the three levels of biodiversity and examples of ecosystem services such as pollination, water purification, and climate regulation.
illustration.caption: Biodiversity includes species, genetic, and ecosystem diversity, all of which provide essential services and resources.

flashcards.definition: A group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring. The most specific level of classification.
flashcards.example: All domestic dogs belong to the species Canis familiaris and can breed with each other.

flashcards.definition: The two-part Latin scientific name given to each species: Genus (capitalised) + species (lowercase). Both italicised.
flashcards.example: Homo sapiens (human); the genus Homo includes extinct human relatives like Homo neanderthalensis.

flashcards.definition: An animal with a backbone (vertebral column) made of vertebrae. Five classes: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals.
flashcards.example: A frog is a vertebrate (amphibian); a spider is NOT — it is an invertebrate (arachnid).

flashcards.definition: An animal without a backbone. Over 95% of all animal species are invertebrates, including arthropods, molluscs, annelids, cnidarians, and echinoderms.
flashcards.example: Insects (beetles, butterflies), spiders, octopuses, earthworms, and jellyfish are all invertebrates.

flashcards.definition: An animal whose body temperature varies with the surrounding environment. Must rely on external heat sources (sun, warm surfaces) to warm up.
flashcards.example: Fish, amphibians, and reptiles are ectothermic. A lizard basks on a rock to raise its body temperature.

flashcards.definition: An animal that generates its own body heat through metabolism and maintains a constant internal temperature regardless of the environment.
flashcards.example: Birds and mammals are endothermic. A human maintains ~37°C whether in the Arctic or the Sahara.

flashcards.definition: A tool for identifying organisms using a series of paired contrasting statements. Each step narrows the possibilities until identification is reached.
flashcards.example: 1a. Has 6 legs → insect; 1b. Has 8 legs → arachnid. Then further questions to identify the specific species.

flashcards.definition: The largest animal phylum: invertebrates with jointed legs, segmented bodies, and a hard chitinous exoskeleton that must be shed (moulted) to grow.
flashcards.example: Insects (6 legs), arachnids (8 legs), crustaceans (10+ legs), and myriapods (many legs) are all arthropods.

flashcards.definition: Eukaryotic organisms with chitin cell walls. Heterotrophic — they secrete enzymes onto food, digest it externally, then absorb nutrients (saprophytic nutrition).
flashcards.example: Mushrooms are the fruiting bodies of fungi; the main body is a network of thread-like hyphae (mycelium) underground.

flashcards.definition: A diverse kingdom of mostly unicellular eukaryotic organisms not fitting into plant, animal, or fungi kingdoms. Includes algae and protozoa.
flashcards.example: Amoeba (moves via pseudopodia), euglena (has chloroplasts AND can feed like an animal), paramecium (covered in cilia).

flashcards.definition: The variety of alleles (gene versions) within a species' gene pool. Higher genetic diversity means greater ability to adapt to environmental changes.
flashcards.example: Cheetahs have very low genetic diversity, making them vulnerable to diseases that could wipe out entire populations.

flashcards.definition: The benefits that humans receive from natural ecosystems — pollination, water purification, climate regulation, soil formation, and nutrient cycling.
flashcards.example: Bees provide pollination services worth billions of dollars annually to global agriculture.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of classification hierarchy from broadest to most specific?
choices: Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum → Kingdom
Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species
Kingdom → Class → Phylum → Order → Family → Genus → Species
Phylum → Kingdom → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species
questions.explanation: Kingdom is the broadest group; species is the most specific. Mnemonic: King Philip Came Over For Good Soup.

questions.stem: Why are viruses not classified in any of the five kingdoms?
choices: They are too small to be classified
They are not considered alive — they have no cellular structure, cannot reproduce independently, and show no life processes outside a host cell
They are a type of bacteria
They belong to the protist kingdom
questions.explanation: Viruses do not meet the criteria for life: they have no cells, no metabolism, and cannot reproduce without hijacking a host cell's machinery. They exist in a grey zone between living and non-living.

questions.stem: A vertebrate has moist skin, lives in water as a larva (with gills) and on land as an adult (with lungs), and lays eggs in water. Which class does it belong to?
questions.explanation: Amphibians undergo metamorphosis — larvae are aquatic with gills, adults are semi-terrestrial with lungs. Their moist skin and water-laid eggs (no shell) are characteristic of this class.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes mammals from all other vertebrate classes?
choices: Females produce milk from mammary glands to feed their young
questions.explanation: Milk production (lactation) is the defining characteristic of mammals. While some mammals lay eggs (platypus, echidna) and some birds breathe air, ONLY mammals produce milk.

questions.stem: A student finds an animal with 8 legs and a body divided into 2 sections. This animal is a(n):
questions.explanation: Arachnids (spiders, scorpions, ticks) have 8 legs and 2 body sections (cephalothorax + abdomen). Insects have 6 legs and 3 body sections.

questions.stem: Two animals have the scientific names Canis lupus and Canis familiaris. What does this tell you about their relationship?
choices: They belong to the same genus (Canis) but are different species — they are closely related
Canis lupus is the ancestor of Canis familiaris
questions.explanation: Sharing the same genus name (Canis) means grey wolves and domestic dogs are closely related. They are different species (lupus vs familiaris) within the same genus.

questions.stem: Use this dichotomous key: 1a. Has wings → 2; 1b. No wings → 3. 2a. Has feathers → Bird; 2b. Has membranous wings → Bat. An organism with wings but NO feathers is a:
questions.explanation: Following the key: has wings (go to 2), does NOT have feathers (2b), so it is a bat. Bats have membranous wings — they are the only mammals capable of true flight.

questions.stem: A fungus, unlike a plant, feeds by:
choices: Engulfing food particles like an amoeba
Secreting enzymes externally onto food and absorbing the digested nutrients (saprophytic nutrition)
Filtering nutrients from water flowing through its body
questions.explanation: Fungi are saprophytes — they release digestive enzymes onto organic matter, break it down externally, then absorb the soluble products. Plants are autotrophic (photosynthesis).

questions.stem: Which animal group has a hard exoskeleton that must be shed (moulted) for the organism to grow?
questions.explanation: Arthropods have a rigid chitin exoskeleton that does not grow. To increase in size, they must shed (moult) the old exoskeleton and form a new, larger one while the new one is still soft.

questions.stem: Why do reptiles not need to keep their skin moist like amphibians do?
choices: Reptiles have dry, scaly skin that is waterproof, reducing water loss — amphibians have thin, moist skin used for gas exchange
Reptiles produce water inside their bodies
Reptiles drink more water than amphibians
questions.explanation: Reptile skin is covered in waterproof keratin scales, preventing dehydration. Amphibian skin is thin and permeable — they use it for supplementary gas exchange, which requires it to stay moist.

questions.stem: What is the advantage of using scientific (binomial) names instead of common names?
choices: Scientific names are easier to remember
Scientific names are universal — one species has one unique name worldwide, avoiding confusion from different common names in different languages and regions
Scientific names describe what the organism tastes like
Scientific names are shorter than common names
questions.explanation: Common names vary by language and region. For example, 'puma,' 'mountain lion,' and 'cougar' all refer to Puma concolor. The binomial name is unique and understood internationally.

questions.stem: Which of these provides an example of an ecosystem service?
choices: A farmer planting wheat in a field
Bees pollinating apple blossoms in an orchard, enabling fruit production
A scientist classifying a new species
questions.explanation: Ecosystem services are benefits humans receive from natural ecosystems without payment. Pollination by wild and managed bees is a critical service — without it, many crops would fail.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between ectothermic and endothermic animals?
choices: Ectotherms are always smaller than endotherms
Ectotherms' body temperature varies with the environment; endotherms generate their own heat to maintain a constant internal temperature
Endotherms live only in cold climates
Ectotherms have backbones; endotherms do not
questions.explanation: Ectotherms ('cold-blooded') depend on external heat sources and their body temperature fluctuates. Endotherms ('warm-blooded') generate heat through metabolism and maintain a stable temperature regardless of surroundings.

questions.stem: Which organisms are classified in the kingdom Protista?
choices: Unicellular eukaryotic organisms like amoeba, euglena, and paramecium
questions.explanation: Protists are a diverse group of mainly unicellular eukaryotes that don't fit neatly into the plant, animal, or fungi kingdoms. Algae are photosynthetic protists; amoeba are animal-like protists (protozoa).

questions.stem: A scientist discovers a new organism. It is unicellular, has a cell wall but no nucleus, and DNA floats free in the cytoplasm. Which kingdom does it belong to?
questions.explanation: The key feature is 'no nucleus' — this means the organism is prokaryotic. Only bacteria (kingdom Monera/Prokaryota) lack a membrane-bound nucleus. All other kingdoms are eukaryotic.
